newsitem.title: PERU: Chronology of Peruvian hostage crisis.
newsitem.headline: Chronology of Peruvian hostage crisis.

text.p: Friday marked one month since Marxist rebels of Peru's Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) stormed the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima, taking more than 500 hostages.
Here is a chronology of the main events:

TUESDAY, Dec. 17 - About 15 heavily armed guerrillas swarm into the Japanese ambassador's home and capture more than 500 people, including government officials and foreign diplomats, attending a cocktail party. The rebels release about 80 women and elderly men in the hours soon after the attack.
WEDNESDAY, Dec. 18 - The guerrillas threaten to kill their hostages unless the government frees up to 500 jailed comrades.
THURSDAY, Dec. 19 - Four ambassadors are released to be a "communications channel" between the rebels and the government.
FRIDAY, Dec. 20 - Rebels release 38 hostages and promise to free another "significant" number.
SATURDAY, Dec. 21 - President Alberto Fujimori says he will study a non-violent "way out" if the guerrillas lay down arms and free all hostages.
SUNDAY, Dec. 22 - The guerrillas release 225 hostages not linked to the government as a "Christmas gesture."
TUESDAY, Dec. 24 - Rebels release Uruguay's ambassador after his country frees two MRTA prisoners.
WEDNESDAY, Dec. 25 - A Japanese diplomat is released due to his delicate health.
THURSDAY, Dec. 26 - Explosion -- believed to be an animal triggering a mine -- at the residence. Later the Guatemalan ambassador is freed.
SATURDAY, Dec. 28 - Government negotiator Domingo Palermo enters the residence for the first face-to-face negotiations with the MRTA. The rebels release 20 hostages.

TUESDAY, Dec. 31 - At the invitation of the rebels, cameramen enter building and interview guerrilla leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini, who reasserts the demand for the release of their jailed comrades. Later the Honduran ambassador and an Argentine diplomat are freed.
WEDNESDAY, Jan. 1 - Rebels release seven captives -- including Peruvian and Japanese businessmen -- lowering hostage total to 74.

TUESDAY, Jan. 7 - Rebel fires two gunshots into the air in the early hours. Fujimori restarts his regular visits to Lima's shantytowns. He says he will not give in to "terrorist blackmail" but vows no "acts of blood." Two employees of Japan's TV Asahi sneak into the residence. Police arrest them when they leave two hours later.
FRIDAY, Jan. 10 - Rebels fire four shots into the air in the early hours. Palermo arranges a second meeting with Cerpa.
SATURDAY, Jan. 11 - Police release the two TV Asahi employees arrested Jan. 7.

SUNDAY, Jan. 12 - Planned meeting between Palermo and Cerpa is called off as rebels insist the talks centre on the release of jailed MRTA members. Palermo proposes a "guarantor commission" made up of the government, MRTA, Red Cross and the Vatican's representative, Peruvian bishop Juan Luis Cipriani.
MONDAY, Jan. 13 - Rebels fire three bursts of gunfire into air during daylight.
WEDNESDAY, Jan. 15 - Rebels accept government proposal for "guarantor" commission and suggest additional representation from Guatemala and a European country.

THURSDAY, Jan. 16 - Government rejects idea of Guatemala as "guarantor" and announces visits to MRTA jailed comrades by relatives or the Red Cross are banned in order not to disturb talks. Cerpa retorts there will be no releases anytime soon because the government is creating obstacles to solving the crisis.
FRIDAY, Jan. 17 - MRTA international spokesman Isaac Velazco specifies in Copenhagen the rebels want Spain or Italy to be a guarantor.
Peruvian government says it is ready to resume face-to-face talks, but will not accept main rebel demand of freedom for 400 jailed comrades.
Rebels free Luis Valencia Hirano, head of the Delta special forces unit of the Peruvian anti-terrorist police, on medical grounds. He is first captive freed in 17 days.
Remaining hostages include Japanese and Bolivian ambassadors, Fujimori's brother Pedro, top Peruvian government and security force officials, and about two dozen Japanese diplomats and businessmen.
